records.sourceFile: Biceps femoris compensates for semitendinosus after ACL reconstruction with a hamstring autograft - A muscle fMRI study in male soccer players.pdf

paper.citation: Tampere T, Victor J, Luyckx T, Vermue H, Arnout N, Witvrouw E, et al. Biceps Femoris Compensates for Semitendinosus After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction With a Hamstring Autograft: A Muscle Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging Study in Male Soccer Players. Am J Sports Med. 2021.
paper.abstract: After ACL reconstruction (ACLR) with a semitendinosus (ST) autograft, male soccer players may have altered hamstring activation. The authors compared exercise-induced T2 shifts on muscle functional MRI between ACLR players and healthy controls, and between operated and contralateral legs, after a prone leg-curl. The biceps femoris long head (BF) showed greater relative activity and the ST less activity in the ACLR group.
paper.tldr: After ACL reconstruction with a hamstring graft, cleared male soccer players used more biceps femoris and less semitendinosus during a prone leg-curl than healthy controls. The authors interpret this as BF partly compensating for ST, a pattern that needs confirmation with running or kicking tasks.
paper.methods: Male soccer players aged 18 to 35 years, cleared for return to play after ST-autograft ACLR (RTP at a mean of 10 months), were compared with healthy controls. Muscle functional MRI (3.0 T, CPMG T2 mapping) was taken before and after a standardized prone leg-curl with 5 kg ankle weights to a Borg score of 20 or loss of motor control. Relative T2 shifts were compared between groups and between operated and contralateral legs, with proportional values normalised to total posterior thigh activity.
paper.findings: Analysed sample: 23 ACLR players and 29 controls. The BF T2 shift was higher in the ACLR group (13.92% vs 8.48%, mean difference 5.44%, P = .003, Cohen d 1.0), and the ST was lower (19.97% vs 25.32%, P = .049). Within the ACLR group, the operated leg showed higher BF (14.54% vs 11.63%, P less than .001) and SM (15.64% vs 13.54%, P = .014) shifts and lower ST shifts (17.31% vs 22.37%, P less than .001) than the contralateral leg. No group differences were found for the gracilis, the SM between groups, total posterior thigh activity or number of leg curls.
paper.limitations: The abstract states that 30 ACLR players and 30 controls were allocated, but results are reported for 23 ACLR players and 29 controls (52 of 60) after scan irregularities and participant exclusions. The authors list multiple surgeons (trained by one senior surgeon, standardized harvest), a limited sample despite an a priori power analysis, male players only at regional and national level, a prone leg-curl that differs from high-speed running, an exercise endpoint based on subjective exertion, and imaging of the long head of biceps only. Many ACLR players also had additional procedures (lateral extra-articular tenodesis in 18, meniscal surgery in 8).
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians treating ACLR players with a hamstring graft may consider muscle-belly-specific assessment of hamstring activation under eccentric load, as the authors suggest, rather than relying on isokinetic strength alone. The study does not establish that training the ST or BF changes outcomes, so any such programme should be justified by its own evidence.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The findings are limited to hamstring activation during a single prone leg-curl in male soccer players after ACLR. They do not test sprinting, kicking or performance outcomes, so they should not be used to set training prescriptions for performance.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study includes players cleared for return to play, about 10 months after surgery, and it supports examining hamstring activation patterns before clearance. It does not show that the pattern predicts re-injury or return to pre-injury performance, so it cannot be used alone as a clearance criterion.

records.sourceFile: Blood Flow Restriction Training Prior to and After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction - A Scoping Review.pdf

paper.citation: Fontanet R, Donat R, Carballeira E. Blood Flow Restriction Training Prior to and After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: A Scoping Review. Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology. 2025;10:450.
paper.abstract: This PRISMA-ScR scoping review of 15 randomized and quasi-randomized trials (417 patients) examines blood flow restriction resistance training before and after ACL reconstruction. Across the included studies, BFR-RT was generally at least as effective as comparison training for strength, muscle size, function and knee pain, and no endurance BFR studies were found.
paper.tldr: Blood flow restriction resistance training before and after ACL reconstruction was at least as effective as comparison training in most of the trials reviewed. The trials are small with mixed quality and no standard BFR protocol, so the authors present it as an interim step rather than a settled standard.
paper.methods: Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR, registered on OSF in April 2024. Six databases (Web of Science, PEDro, Scopus, PubMed, SportDiscus, Cochrane) were searched to 24 September 2025, with citation chasing and grey literature. Eligible studies were RCTs or quasi-RCTs of BFR combined with resistance or endurance exercise in ACL reconstruction patients with autografts. Quality was rated with PEDro, and exercise reporting with CERT; quantitative synthesis was judged not feasible.
paper.findings: Fifteen studies were included, with 417 patients. 2 of 5 preoperative and 5 of 9 postoperative studies reported superior BFR-RT outcomes, and the rest reported comparable outcomes. Reported BFR-RT benefits included muscle size, strength, endurance, knee pain, self-report scores and lower serum Atrogin-1 and MuRF1 in one study, and one trial found return to sport 1.4 months sooner with low-load BFR than low-load training alone. Low-load BFR gave a faster reduction in knee pain than heavy-load training in three trials, but caused more pain during training in one.
paper.limitations: The review is a scoping map with no pooled effect size, and data could not be extracted from several studies. PEDro scores were modest (median 6.87, IQR 6-8), and most studies did not blind participants or therapists. The conclusions state that preoperative BFR-RT significantly increased strength and endurance compared with low-load training, while the discussion reports superior outcomes in only 2 of 5 preoperative studies, so the conclusions read more strongly than the study-level results; the pain-during-training finding is also described as knee pain in the discussion but muscle pain in the results.
paper.practicalImplications: BFR resistance training is a reasonable option for limiting quadriceps loss or managing knee pain before and after ACL reconstruction, particularly when heavy loads are poorly tolerated or weight bearing is limited. Set cuff pressure relative to measured limb occlusion pressure and prefer supervised sessions, since unsupervised home-based protocols generally showed less significant improvements. Expect results comparable to heavy-load training in most trials rather than clear superiority, and screen for thromboembolism risk, as the included trials largely excluded high-risk patients.
paper.athleteDev: BFR resistance training may help maintain or rebuild lower-limb strength and muscle size with lighter loads in athletes rehabilitating an ACL. The evidence comes from ACL reconstruction patients rather than athletes training for performance, so it does not show a performance gain.
paper.rtp: The review supports BFR resistance training as an add-on in early ACL rehabilitation, including when weight bearing is limited. Return-to-activity time was reported in only two trials: one found return to sport 1.4 months sooner with low-load BFR than low-load training, and the other found no difference between BFR with heavy loads and heavy-load training alone. Reinjury and long-term function were not studied, so it cannot set return-to-sport criteria or timelines.

records.sourceFile: Calf strains in athletes - A narrative review of management, injury grading, and return to sport.pdf

paper.citation: Pagan-Rosado R, Troyer W, Rosario-Concepcion R, Feaster B, Encalada S, Kindle B, et al. Calf strains in athletes: a narrative review of management, injury grading, and return to sport. Sports Med Open. 2025;11:158.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of imaging and injury grading as predictors of return to sport after calf strains in athletes. Eleven included studies, mainly retrospective, suggest that ultrasound and MRI give useful information on injury severity and recovery time, that different grading systems correlate with outcomes, and that no single modality or grading system is clearly superior.
paper.tldr: Ultrasound and MRI help grade calf strains and give a rough sense of recovery time, but no imaging grade reliably decides return to play. Clinical assessment remains the basis of return-to-play decisions, with imaging as a supplement.
paper.methods: Self-described narrative review following the SANRA guideline, with selected PRISMA 2020 elements and a librarian-designed Boolean search of PubMed and Scopus. Thirty-one articles were retrieved and 11 met the inclusion criteria (human calf muscle injuries, MRI or ultrasound grading, and return-to-play outcomes). Screening was done by four investigators, and no risk-of-bias or certainty-of-evidence grading was performed.
paper.findings: The review text gives an overall return-to-play range of 2 to 102 days with a mean of 39 ± 18 days, but Table 2 attributes the 2 to 102 day range to Green et al. (index injuries, Australian football) and the 39 ± 18 day mean to Pedret et al. (medial gastrocnemius tears). In Australian football players, injuries with no, mild and severe aponeurotic disruption took a mean of 19.4, 26.7 and 31.3 days to return to play, and in Premiership rugby players myofascial-interface injuries returned to full training in a mean of 20.1 days versus 46.8 days for tendon or aponeurosis injuries (p = 0.02). The authors state that no specific imaging factor has been linked to return to play, and that the classifications studied correlated with return-to-play time without one being clearly superior.
paper.limitations: Most included studies were retrospective, study sizes ranged from 10 to 184 injuries, and seven of eleven studies had fewer than 50 injuries with complete imaging data. Imaging protocols and return-to-play definitions varied, and only two studies assessed interobserver reliability, which was fair to moderate. The text has internal conflicts: the search date (June 2024 in the Abstract, 10 October 2025 in the Methods), the number of MRI studies (eight in the Discussion, nine in the Limitations), the source of the 2 to 102 day and 39 day figures, and the Key Points' return-to-play range of 2 to 12 weeks.
paper.practicalImplications: Use MRI or ultrasound to grade a calf strain and to flag features such as aponeurotic disruption or asynchronous gastrocnemius-soleus movement, which were linked to longer recovery in the included studies. Do not set a return date from the imaging grade alone, since the authors conclude that imaging should supplement the clinical examination.
paper.athleteDev: Use imaging grade and location as context for expected time loss when planning a calf-strain return, and avoid treating a single grade as a fixed return date. The studies come mainly from professional football and rugby, so the timelines may not transfer to other sports or to recreational athletes.
paper.rtp: This review is directly about return to sport, but it cannot support a clearance decision by itself. The authors state that clinical examination (absence of palpation pain, calf strength and sport-specific activity without symptoms) remains the gold standard, with imaging used to support those decisions.

records.sourceFile: Characteristics and outcomes of athletes with slow recovery from sports-related concussion - A CARE Consortium Study.pdf

paper.citation: McAllister TW, Broglio SP, Katz BP, Perkins SM, LaPradd M, Zhou W, et al. Characteristics and Outcomes of Athletes With Slow Recovery From Sports-Related Concussion: A CARE Consortium Study. Neurology. 2023;100(14):e1510-e1519.
paper.abstract: This prospective multisite study followed 1,751 concussed collegiate athletes and defined slow recovery as taking at least 14 days to become asymptomatic or 24 days to return to play, slower than about 80% of peers. Slow recovery applied to 399 athletes (22.8%), who were more often female and had higher early symptom burden than typical recoverers. The authors conclude that most slow recoverers returned to play within months, which they present as a reassuring prognosis.
paper.tldr: About one in five concussed collegiate athletes recovered slowly, and most of those returned to play within about two months. Sex and early symptom scores did not predict return among slow recoverers, and about 1 in 10 had not returned by 6 months.
paper.methods: Prospective observational cohort at 26 civilian universities and four service academies, with baseline testing, daily symptom reports for 14 days, and assessments at five postinjury points through 6 months. Slow recovery was defined by time to the asymptomatic point and to return to play, analyzed with Kaplan-Meier curves and Cox proportional hazards models.
paper.findings: Slow-recovery athletes were more often female (41.1% vs 35.6%, P=.05), reported more prior concussions (0.72 vs 0.59, P=.03), had higher postinjury SCAT symptom scores (36.6 vs 25.4, P<.001), worse postinjury SAC and BESS scores, lower compliance with daily symptom checks in the first 14 days (48.8% vs 67.9%), and were more often injured in practice (70.7% vs 65.1%, P=.04). In the slow group, median return to play was 34.7 days, with 77.6% returned by 60 days and 83.4% by 88 days, and 10.6% (2.4% of the whole cohort) had not returned by 180 days. Within the slow group no candidate predictor reached P<.05; prior concussion history was borderline (HR 0.90, P=.05) and all C-statistics were 0.49 to 0.53.
paper.limitations: The slow group is defined by cut-offs taken from the cohort's own timing distribution, 73 athletes were censored, and missing dates were imputed for 292 athletes. Nearly half the slow group's postinjury BSI values were missing (46%), and results apply only to collegiate varsity athletes and cadets. The text has internal inconsistencies: the abstract gives 83.4% returning within 90 days as n = 349, which is 87.5% of 399, and the Discussion says slow recoverers were more often injured in noncontact or limited-contact sport although the sport-category difference was not significant (P=.12).
paper.practicalImplications: Use these figures to set expectations with slow recoverers (athletes taking at least 14 days to become asymptomatic or 24 days to return to play): most returned within about two months, but about 10% had not returned by six months. Do not use sex or early symptom scores to predict an individual athlete's timeline, because they did not predict return within the slow group.
paper.athleteDev: This study concerns concussion recovery timelines rather than training or performance, so it has no direct performance application. It should not be used to plan training loads for athletes returning from concussion, since it reports no load or performance outcome.
paper.rtp: Useful for setting expectations: 77.6% of slow recoverers returned to play within 60 days and 10.6% had not returned by six months, and the return curve flattened after about 60 days. It cannot set return-to-play criteria or predict an individual's course, and clearance in the study rested on the treating clinician's examination.

records.sourceFile: Clinical and biomechanical outcomes of rehabilitation targeting intersegmental control in athletic groin pain- prospective cohort of 205 patients.pdf

paper.citation: King E, Franklyn-Miller A, Richter C, O'Reilly E, Doolan M, Moran K, et al. Clinical and biomechanical outcomes of rehabilitation targeting intersegmental control in athletic groin pain: prospective cohort of 205 patients. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52:1054-1062.
paper.abstract: This prospective, uncontrolled study followed 205 male patients with athletic groin pain through a three-level rehabilitation programme targeting intersegmental control. HAGOS scores improved on all subscales, 73% returned to play pain-free at a mean of 9.9 weeks, and cutting biomechanics changed, including greater pelvic rotation towards the direction of travel. The authors suggest the approach is an alternative to anatomically specific rehabilitation and warrants randomised comparison.
paper.tldr: In 205 male athletes with groin pain, a programme that trained coordination between the trunk, pelvis and legs was followed by 73% pain-free return to play in about 10 weeks. With no control group, treat this as a promising programme to test against standard care, not as proof that it works better.
paper.methods: Prospective uncontrolled series of consecutive male patients seen at one Dublin sports clinic from January 2013 to May 2015; 205 of 322 assessed patients were eligible. Patients had a clinical examination, including squeeze and crossover tests, a 110-degree cutting task with 3D analysis, and a three-level rehabilitation programme covering intersegmental control and strength, linear running, and multidirectional drills. The primary outcome was HAGOS, with pain-free return to play, squeeze test and 3D cutting biomechanics as secondary outcomes, analysed with paired t tests and statistical parametric mapping.
paper.findings: Of 150 patients with repeat HAGOS scores, all six subscales improved, for example pain from 72.9 to 88.0 and sport from 50.7 to 86.3 (effect sizes 0.59 to 1.78, p < 0.001). Pain-free squeeze at 0, 45 and 90 degrees was achieved by 94% (105 of 112) at discharge, and pain-free return to play occurred in 73% (150 of 205) after a mean of 9.9 weeks, with no difference by anatomical diagnosis (p = 0.56). In the cutting analysis (n = 112), the largest within-group changes were greater thorax side flexion (effect size 0.79) and pelvic rotation (0.76) towards the direction of travel, with ankle work increasing and hip work decreasing.
paper.limitations: The study has no control group and was not randomised, with 27% lost before the repeat HAGOS and a further 14% returning to play without the final 3D test, and re-injury is not reported. The abstract gives squeeze effect sizes of 0.49 to 0.68 while Table 3 gives 0.46 to 0.68, and return time SD is 3.5 weeks in the abstract and 3.4 in the Discussion; table values are used here. The comparisons with faster return than earlier randomised trials are across studies, and the clinic declares it operates an athletic groin pain programme.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest that rehabilitation for groin pain can target coordination between body segments rather than one anatomical structure, and that 3D cutting analysis can identify specific targets. Because there is no control group, use the programme as a structured option with clear progression goals, not as a proven superior approach.
paper.athleteDev: The authors link cutting strategy to cutting performance and to groin pain risk, and suggest movement strategy may be part of the injury mechanism. The study does not measure performance outcomes directly, so treat movement-pattern findings as a reason to monitor cutting mechanics, not as a training target on their own.
paper.rtp: This study is directly relevant to return to sport: 73% of field-sport athletes returned pain-free after a mean of 9.9 weeks. Clearance was based on completing all three rehabilitation levels with symptom-free linear and multidirectional drills; squeeze testing and repeat 3D analysis guided further follow-up, and 7 patients returned with residual squeeze symptoms. It cannot show that the programme beats standard care because there is no control group, and re-injury after return is not reported.
